A Deep-DiD Method to Estimate Heterogeneous Treatment Effects: Application to Content Creator Selection

Yan Cheng,a,* Jingbo Wang,b,* Xinyu Cao,b,* Zuo-Jun Max Shen,c Yuhui Zhangd

1. Introduction Difference-in-Difference (DiD) is a commonly used method to estimate the average treatment effect on the treated in a quasi-experimental setting, with the key identifying assumption that the average outcome in the treated and control groups would have fol lowed parallel trends in the absence of treatment (Roth et al. 2023). However, this estimate only allows us to understand whether and by how much an inter vention is effective on average. The explosion of data now makes it possible to explore how treatment effects vary across individuals with different charac teristics. By understanding how individuals respond to interventions differently, companies can customize their interventions to maximize effectiveness. Thus, estimating heterogeneous treatment effects (HTEs) can significantly enhance various marketing practices,

such as pricing strategies, product recommendations, and marketing campaign optimization (see, e.g., Fong et al. 2015, Ascarza 2018, and Hitsch et al. 2024).

Although the availability of rich data allows for high-dimensional pretreatment features, estimating HTEs parametrically becomes more challenging because there can be complex interactions between pretreatment features, and it is difficult to assume a correct functional relationship between HTEs and pre treatment features. Existing works have proposed sev eral nonparametric approaches for the estimation of HTEs, including Bayesian nonparametric methods (see, e.g., Hill 2011) and tree-based methods (see, e.g., Wager and Athey 2018).

Farrell et al. (2021) demonstrated the use of DNN for estimating causal parameters, and Farrell et al. (2020) presented a DNN-based framework that can

Page 2

estimate fully flexible nonparametric individual het erogeneity. Inspired by these works, we integrate deep neural networks (DNN) in a DiD framework to estimate HTEs. We propose a dual-network archi tecture consisting of two DNN structures. One DNN structure captures the nonparametric relationship between the treatment effect β(·) and pretreatment fea tures Wi. The other DNN structure summarizes high- dimensional individual fixed effects µi and time fixed effects τt into a nuisance function f(µi,τt), which also allows for possible interactions between them. The combination of these two parts forms a semipara metric DiD model with DNNs embedded. We name it the Deep-DiD model.

Through simulations, we demonstrate that our Deep- DiD method can uncover the true HTEs with high accuracy across various functional forms of the true β(·) and f(·,·). We also show that the embedded DNN structures demonstrate more robust estimation perfor mance than linear estimators and random forests. We further examine how the estimation performance of our approach varies with sample sizes, feature dimen sions, and different implementation choices. Overall, our Deep-DiD method demonstrates high accuracy and robustness in estimation.

We apply our method to an empirical setting in which a large video-sharing platform launched a “Creator Signing Program” (“the signing program” hereafter) aimed at identifying promising creators and encouraging them to produce more high-quality con tent. The program was initially launched in three countries located in South America, Africa, and Europe.1 Signed creators received monthly payments based on their performance. We apply our method to estimate the HTEs of the signing program and further demonstrate how our estimation can aid the platform in optimizing creator selection.

We construct a matched data set with 2,343 creators who were signed from May 1–June 30, 2022 (the trea ted group) and 2,343 creators who remained unsigned (the control group). For each creator, we observed their activities in the 89 days before and 90 days after the signing date.2 We define two performance mea sures: the total user viewing time contributed by the creator’s videos and the total user engagement con tributed by the creators’ videos. The two groups show parallel trends in daily average performance measures before treatment. Using a canonical DiD model, we show that the signing program substantially boosts the performance metrics of signed creators.

We further prepare the data for estimating the Deep-DiD model and testing its performance in crea tor selection. We construct a set of variables (Wi) that describe creators’ pretreatment characteristics in three aspects: Creator Production and Viewer Responses, Visual Features, and Audio Features. Because of the

loss of some video data, the data set with the full set of pretreatment features contains 2,204 creators, with 1,126 from the treated group and 1,078 from the con trol group. We randomly split this data set into two parts: 60% (1,322 creators) for model training and validation and 40% (882 creators) for out-of-sample testing. The trained model provides an estimated function ˆβ(·), which we can apply to calculate ˆβi 

ˆβ(Wi) for each i in both the training-validation and test sets. The estimated treatment effects reveal sub stantial heterogeneity across creators.

Our method can help the platform optimize creator selection. By utilizing our estimated function β(Wi) and each creator’s pretreatment features Wi, the plat form can estimate how much the signing program will change the performance of each creator. The plat form can then select the creators with the highest esti mated treatment effects to sign.

We evaluate this creator selection method through out-of-sample tests. Among the 882 creators in the test set, 441 were signed by the platform (labeled “Platform Selected”). We also select 441 creators with the highest estimated treatment effects (labeled “Model Selected”) and compare them with the Platform Selected ones. The Model Selected creators show signifi cantly higher estimated treatment effects compared with the Platform Selected creators. Furthermore, among creators signed by the platform, those selected by the model demonstrate substantially higher actual perfor mance jumps compared with those not selected by the model. Here, a creator’s performance jump is defined as his or her daily average performance after the signing date minus that before the signing date. This measure can be considered an “empirically observed” treatment effect of the signing program on signed creators, although it is not strictly causal. These two evaluation results collectively demonstrate that creator selection based on our Deep-DiD method outperforms the plat form’s selection. We also show that creator selection based on our Deep-DiD method consistently performs better than selection based on linear models.

1.1. Contributions to Literature Methodologically, our paper contributes to the liter ature on machine-learning-based causal inference. Machine-learning-based causal inference methods are advancing rapidly, driven by the availability of big data and powerful computing platforms. These advancements enable researchers and practitioners to examine new empirical scenarios that go beyond the capabilities of traditional methods. For instance, they allow for the handling of high-dimensional covariates (Belloni et al. 2017) and the estimation of heteroge neous treatment effects for optimal targeting (Hitsch et al. 2024). Wager and Athey (2018) proposed to estimate heterogeneous treatment effects using

Page 3

random forests. Applying this method, Guo et al. (2021) estimated the heterogeneous treatment effects of the Physician Payment Sunshine Act disclosure on pharma ceutical payments to doctors, whereas Zhang and Luo (2023) estimated the relationship between photos posted by consumers and restaurant survival. Cong et al. (2021) employed the orthogonal random forest method pro posed by Oprescu et al. (2019) to estimate the heteroge neous treatment effect of livestreaming.

As a significant recent development in this field, Farrell et al. (2021) demonstrated the use of DNNs for estimating causal parameters. They further extended it to estimate heterogeneous treatment effects Farrell et al. (2020). To the best of our knowledge, our paper is the first empirical study to implement the DNN-based heterogeneity architecture proposed in Farrell et al. (2020). We innovatively propose a dual-network structure that combines two DNNs in a DiD framework, enabling estimation of HTEs with both high-dimensional pretreatment features and high-dimensional fixed effects. Through simulations and an empirical applica tion, we demonstrate the robust and superior perfor mance of this DNN-based approach.

Our paper also contributes to the literature on mod ern variations of DiD methods that deal with hetero geneous treatment effects. Two-way fixed-effects (TWFE) estimator is a DiD estimator that accounts for both unit-specific and time-specific unobserved het erogeneity in panel data by including fixed effects for units (e.g., individuals, firms, states) and time periods. Chaisemartin and D’Haultfœuille (2020) examined the properties of TWFE estimators, demonstrating that the TWFE estimators can produce misleading esti mates when treatment effects vary across units or over time. This is because TWFE estimators calculate a weighted sum of treatment effects, where some weights can be negative when the actual treatment effects vary across units or over time. There are sev eral methodological works trying to deal with the bias

in TWFE when HTE exists. Callaway and Sant’Anna (2021) proposed a group-time ATT (average treatment effect on the treated) estimator that computes the average treatment effect for each cohort and time period and then aggregates them using inverse proba bility weighting or outcome regression. Sun and Abra ham (2021) fixed TWFE’s biases by first estimating cohort-specific dynamic effects and then combined these effects to produce ATT. Borusyak et al. (2024) proposed an imputation-based estimator; it predicted counterfactual outcomes for treated units by estimat ing a linear factor model using untreated units only and then computed treatment effects by comparing the observed and predicted outcomes of treated units. All of these methods required parallel trends (i.e., in the absence of treatment, the average outcome of the treated and control groups would have followed the same trajectory over time) and no anticipatory effects (i.e., treatment effects do not occur before the actual treatment date) as key identification assumptions. Abadie and Gardeazabal (2003) and Abadie et al. (2010) proposed a synthetic control method that esti mated the treatment effect on a single (or a few) trea ted unit(s) by constructing a weighted combination of untreated units that closely mimicked the treated unit’s pretreatment outcomes and characteristics. Note that although the synthetic control method can deal with violation of the parallel-trend assumption, it is restricted to settings with a single or small number of treated units, and it is not suited when treated units’ outcomes are outside the range of those for control units (Arkhangelsky et al. 2021, Li et al. 2024). Arkhan gelsky et al. (2021) hybridized DiD and synthetic con trol method so that it could handle settings with many treated units or when treated and control units were very different. It also solved the biases in TWFE esti mators when treatment effects varied across units or over time. Table 1 summarizes the papers mentioned above.

Our paper is most closely related to Borusyak et al. (2024) because both approaches can directly estimate individual-level HTEs. Our DNN-based method can be understood, at a high level, as a generalization of the imputation-based approach proposed by Boru syak et al. (2024). Unlike Borusyak et al. (2024), which imputed untreated counterfactuals for treated units by estimating a linear factor model, our method uses DNN to nonparametrically impute untreated counter factuals for treated units. DNN not only allows for more flexible imputations but also enables our method to handle high-dimensional covariates.

This paper is broadly related to the literature on the application of deep learning methods in marketing pro blems. For example, Liu et al. (2019) employed deep learning-based natural language processing to analyze how consumers utilize review content; Wei and Jiang (2022) demonstrated that deep neural networks can accurately estimate structural parameters with low esti mation costs; Cao et al. (2025) utilized a deep learning approach to examine the impact of image-text coupling on consumer preference; Fong et al. (2022) developed an explainable deep learning classifier to predict emo tional responses to music. Several studies have utilized deep learning approaches to understand the influence of images (see, e.g., Li and Xie 2020, Liu et al. 2020, Dew et al. 2022, Zhang et al. 2022, Dzyabura et al. 2023, and Zhang and Luo 2023) and videos (see, e.g., Li et al. 2019, Zhou et al. 2021, Cheng and Zhang 2024, and Yang et al. 2025) on consumer perceptions, preferences, and purchase decisions. Liu (2023) provided a compre hensive review in this area. Again, as far as we know, our paper represents the first empirical application of deep learning in estimating heterogeneous treatment effects. Furthermore, we incorporate visual features and audio features, which are derived from unstruc tured video data using deep-learning-based methods, as inputs in our Deep-DiD model.

Substantively, this paper contributes to the litera ture on content-sharing platforms, particularly regard ing content creation. Existing works have empirically studied how to motivate more content creation using financial incentives and behavioral nudges (Burtch et al. 2018, Huang et al. 2019, Zeng et al. 2022, Lu et al. 2023) and have theoretically examined how platforms should compensate creators to motivate content creations (Jain and Qian 2021, Bhargava 2022). To the best of our knowledge, our paper is the first to quantify the causal impact of signing creators on their performances. Fur thermore, we propose an approach based on deep neu ral networks that allows platforms to optimally select creators based on their comprehensive characteristics.

This paper is also related to the literature on influ encer marketing and the creator economy. With the rapid growth of influencer marketing in recent years,3

there has been a surge in research studying various

aspects of influencer marketing. This includes investi gations into the impact of brand sponsorship on influ encers’ reputation (Cheng and Zhang 2024), how influencers adjust their voices in sponsored videos (Hwang et al. 2021), the effect of live-streaming on product demand and seller survival (Cong et al. 2021, Liu et al. 2022, Huang and Morozov 2025), and the relationship between audience size and live-streaming revenues (Lu et al. 2021). Several studies have also examined influencer selection. Yang et al. (2025) pro posed a motion-related metric that predicts the effec tiveness of influencer ads on product sales, whereas Rajaram and Manchanda (2021) used an interpretable deep learning framework to predict the popularity of influencers’ content. Leung et al. (2022) explored the factors that determine the effectiveness of influencer marketing, whereas Wies et al. (2023) and Tian et al. (2024) proposed influencer selection methods based on the number of followers and follower elasticity. Feng et al. (2025) predicted the potential of influencers using their facial features. It is worth noting that these studies primarily consider the influencer selection problem from the perspective of sponsoring compa nies, proposing metrics for selecting influencers. In contrast, the empirical application in this paper focuses on the creator selection problem from the platform’s perspective; how should a platform select creators to sign and provide financial incentives? We utilize data from a real signing program to estimate the causal effects and propose a creator selection method based on the estimated HTEs. When estimating the HTEs, we make use of comprehensive characteristics of creators rather than relying on a few metrics.

The paper is structured as follows. Section 2 intro duces the Deep-DiD method and shows its perfor mance through simulations. Section 3 provides an introduction to the empirical context. In Section 4, we apply our Deep-DiD method to estimate the heteroge neous treatment effects of the signing program. Sec tion 5 illustrates how to conduct creator selection using our model estimation results and evaluates the performance of model-based creator selection. Section 6 offers concluding remarks for the paper.

2. Deep-DiD Method Difference-in-Difference (DiD) is a widely used method for estimating causal effects in quasi-experimental set tings. The idea is to compare the difference in outcomes after and before the treatment for the treated group to that of the untreated group. The key identifying assump tion is that the treated and untreated groups exhibit parallel trends in the outcome measure before treat ment, and the parallel trajectory would have continued in the absence of treatment. A canonical DiD setup is

Yit  βDi × At + µi + τt + ɛit, (1)

Cheng et al.: A Deep-DiD Method to Estimate Heterogeneous Treatment Effects Marketing Science, 2026, vol. 45, no. 2, pp. 258–279, © 2026 INFORMS 261

Page 5

where Yit denotes the outcome of interest for individ ual i at time t (i  1,:::,N,t  1,:::,T). The binary vari able Di indicates whether individual i belongs to the treated group (Di  1) or the control group (Di  0). The binary variable At denotes whether the treatment has been launched by time t. µi and τt capture individual and time fixed effects, respectively. ɛit is the error term. The interaction term’s coefficient β captures the average treatment effect on the treated (ATT) (Bertrand et al. 2004). Nowadays, more and more marketing applications require the estimation of heterogeneous treatment effects, that is, to predict how each individual would react to the treatment and how the treatment effect varies with their pretreatment features. In the DiD framework, it is essential to estimate β(·) as a function of Wi in the following equation:

Yit  β(Wi)Di × At + µi + τt + ɛit, (2)

equation / math rendering (image)

where Wi is a J-dimensional vector denoting individ ual i’s pretreatment features. β(Wi) captures the aver age treatment effect conditional on the pretreatment features.

An earlier practice of estimating heterogeneous treatment effect is to assume a functional form of β(Wi) and estimate it accordingly. For example, there are existing works, including three-way interactions Di × At × Wi in the DiD model, to examine treatment effect heterogeneity (see, e.g., Duflo 2003), which is equivalent to assuming β(Wi) as a linear function of Wi. However, there can be complex interactions between these pretreatment features. A linear func tional form of β(Wi) cannot take into account the possible complex interactions between pretreatment features, and it is hard for researchers to know the cor rect specification ex ante. Therefore, this method may give a directional sense of how the treatment effect

changes with a certain variable, but it may lead to biased estimates if the goal is to obtain an accurate estimate of individual-level HTEs.

Nonparametric approaches to estimation of hetero geneous treatment effects include nearest-neighbor matching, kernel methods, and series estimation. As the dimension of pretreatment features gets large, the performance of these methods deteriorates (Wager and Athey 2018), and it calls for the utilization of machine-learning methods. Wager and Athey (2018) and Athey et al. (2019) proposed to estimate heteroge neous treatment effects using random forests.

Farrell et al. (2021) showed that deep neural net works (DNN) can be used in semiparametric infer ence. More specifically, they showed that DNN can be used to estimate the nonparametric part (they call it a “nuisance function”) in the first-step estimation with a fast enough convergence rate, which enables a valid second-step inference4 of the parametric part. They showed the application of this method on estimating average causal parameters. Farrell et al. (2020) further presented a DNN-based framework that could estimate fully flexible nonparametric individual heterogeneity.

Inspired by this line of works, we innovatively inte grate DNN with the DiD model to estimate β(Wi). We call it the Deep-DiD approach. We consider a more general setup, where the individual fixed effects and time fixed effects may interact and are represented by a general functional form f(µi,τt):

Yit  β(Wi)Di × At + f(µi,τt) + ɛit: (3)

Figure 1 illustrates the conceptual framework of our approach. We use a dual-network architecture in esti mation. One is the HTE estimation network, with Wi as the input layer and βi as the output layer. This DNN characterizes βi as a nonparametric function of Wi. The other is the fixed-effect network, with the

Figure 1. Deep-DiD Model Architecture

Cheng et al.: A Deep-DiD Method to Estimate Heterogeneous Treatment Effects 262 Marketing Science, 2026, vol. 45, no. 2, pp. 258–279, © 2026 INFORMS

Page 6

high-dimensional individual dummies and time-period dummies as the input layer and a nuisance function f(µi,τt) as the parametric layer.5 As we will show in Section 2.1.2, this design allows for possible complex interactions between individual fixed effects and time fixed effects.

The estimation process is an iterative process. In each iteration, the mean squared loss between the outcome variable yit and the sum of β(Wi)Di × At and f(µi,τt) are computed, and then the parameters in each layer are updated to minimize this loss in the next iteration until convergence is achieved. The heterogeneous treat ment effects βi  β(Wi)’s are retrieved from the para metric layer of the HTE estimation network.

2.1. Simulation We conduct a series of simulations to demonstrate the performance of our Deep-DiD method. In particular, in a DiD setup with heterogeneous treatment effects as described by Equation (3), our Deep-DiD method can recover the true distribution of β(Wi) with high enough accuracy.

2.1.1. Simulation Procedure. Let us first describe the data-generating process. We generate (Wi,µi,τt,Di,At) (i  1,:::,N,t  1,:::,T), where Wi is a J-dimensional vector, according to certain distribution assumptions. Unless otherwise specified, we assume that each element in Wi is independent and follows a normal distribution N(5,3). Individual fixed effects µi are all independent and follow a normal distribution N(0,5) (i  1,:::,N). Time fixed effects τt are also indepen dent and follow N(0,1) (t  1,:::,T). We consider a setting that the treatment assignment is based on observables rather than random, which makes the estimation task more challenging. In particular, we assume that each individual i is treated with probability Pr(Di  1)  (1 + exp(P

j(Wij 5)=J))1. We assume that the treatment takes place at T=2, that is, At  1 when t ≥T=2, and At  0 otherwise. The error terms ɛit are independent and follow N(0,1).6 Then, we compute βi  β(Wi) and f(µi,τt) according to the assumed func tional forms and compute Yit according to Equation (3). (Wi,Yit,Di,At) (i  1,:::,N,t  1,:::,T) constitutes a panel data for model training. (Note that µi and τt are unobserved.) Following the same procedure, we gen erate another data set with the same size. This is a test data set, which is independent with the training data set and will be used to evaluate the estimation performance.

For the training data set, we further randomly split it into 80% for model training and 20% for validation. We use the training set to train the model and use MSE loss on the validation set to monitor the training progress to prevent overfitting. In both networks, we

design two hidden layers. Unless otherwise specified, we set each hidden layer with 32 neurons. Rectified linear unit (ReLU) activation functions are used between layers, which is a common and effective choice for neural network architectures. We set the batch size as 512 and the number of epochs as 10. We use the Adaptive Moment Estimation (Adam) opti mizer. The learning rate is initialized at 0.001 and halved if the model’s performance fails to improve for two consecutive evaluation periods.7

The trained model essentially provides us with an estimated (nonparametric) function ˆβ(·). We apply it to the test set to calculate ˆβi  ˆβ(Wi) for each i in the test set. To evaluate the estimation performance, we compare the distribution of ˆβis to the distribution of true βis of the test sample. We employ two commonly used metrics to quantify the difference between the two distributions: the Kolmogorov-Smirnov (KS) Sta tistic and the Jensen-Shannon (JS) Divergence. The KS Statistic, ranging from 0 to 1, represents the maximum vertical distance between the two cumulative distribu tion functions (CDFs) and is widely used in statistical analysis. The JS Divergence, also ranging from 0 to 1 when implemented in Python Scipy, is a symmetrized and smoothed version of the Kullback-Leibler diver gence. For both metrics, lower values indicate greater similarity between the two distributions.8 To further evaluate whether our method accurately predicts the value of each βi (beyond distribution matching), we also use a third metric: Normalized Root Mean Square

Error (NRMSE)

=σβ, which is the root of mean square error divided by the standard deviation. Whereas both mean squared error (MSE) and root mean squared error (RMSE) depend on the scale of the variable of interest, making it hard to eval uate and compare the estimation performance across different tasks, NRMSE is scale independent and comparable across different data sets with different scales. It is usually considered an excellent fit when NRMSE<0.1.

All simulations are conducted on a local Windows 11 desktop with an Intel Core i9-14900KF processor and an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4090 graphics card (24GB VRAM). The Python environment comprised CUDA 11.8, PyTorch 2.3.1, and Python 3.10.14.

2.1.2. Simulation Results. Performance of Deep-DiD Under Various Settings. First, we show that under different assumptions for the true functional forms of β(·) and f(·,·), the true βis can be well uncovered using our Deep-DiD method (Figure 2). We try two different assumptions for the true functional forms of β(·) (linear, nonlinear) and three for f(·,·) (additive, multiplicative, and cyclical).

There are 2 × 3  6 combinations in total. The detailed specifications are listed in the note of Figure 2. The results demonstrate that the true βis can be estimated accurately across different functional forms of the het erogeneous treatment effect β(·) and fixed effects f(·,·).

Second, we test the performance of our approach under different sample sizes (N, T) and feature dimen sions (J). In Figure 3(a), we vary the number of indivi duals N ∈{1,500, 3,000, 6,000} and the number of time periods T ∈{20,90}, with J fixed at 100. The estimation is fairly accurate for all the combinations. A general trend is that when the number of individuals increases (from left to right) or when the number of time periods increases (from top to bottom), the estimation becomes more accurate. Note that for the case of (N1,500, T20), we increase the number of epochs to 20 to achieve satisfactory performance, whereas the number of epochs is set to 10 in other cases. This suggests that a higher number of epochs is required when working with fewer observations. In Figure 3(b), we vary the number of individuals N ∈{1,500, 3,000, 6,000}, and the dimension of pretreatment features J ∈{100,300}, with T fixed at 90. The estimation performance improves when N becomes larger but is not sensitive to the change in J.

Third, we examine what happens if there are two different groups of individuals drawn from different distributions. In particular, we assume half of the pop ulation is a high-performing population, with each element in Wi drawn from N(8,3) and individual fixed effects µi drawn from N(2,5); the other half of the population is low-performing, with each element

in Wi drawn from N(5,3) and individual fixed effects µi drawn from N(0,5). We assume that each individ ual i is treated with probability Pr(Di  1)  1=[1+ exp(MinMax(Wi1+Wi2+Wi3+µi))], where MinMax(·) means a min-max normalization function. Note that the assumed Pr(Di  1) increases with Wi1 + Wi2+ Wi3 + µi, so the treated group will consist of more individuals from the high-performing population, and the control group will consist of more from the low-performing population. This reflects the case when there is systematic difference between the treated and control groups, and the difference is contributed by both observable and unobservable features.9 As shown in Figure 4(a), our model estimation can still uncover the true distribution of βis in this case. In addi tion, we consider the case when there is also a shift in time fixed effects τt, which reflects time-variant con founders that affect all individuals equally or ran domly. Specifically, we assume that τt follows N(0,1) before treatment and N(2,1) after treatment. The model estimation still performs well, as shown in Figure 4(b).

Fourth, we examine the performance of our approach across different implementation choices in the estimation procedure: the optimizer {Adam, SGD} (SGD stands for stochastic gradient descent), the num ber of notes in each layer of the DNN {32, 64}, the batch size {512, 1024}, the learning rate {0.001, 0.005}, and the number of epochs {5, 10}.10 Table 2 shows the estimation performance (i.e., KS statistic, JS diver gence, and NRMSE, all calculated on the test set) under different parameter values. Deep-DiD vs. Linear Model and Random Forests. Next, we compare the performance of Deep-DiD method versus representative existing approaches.

We first show that our method has more robust per formance than a conventional parametric approach; that is, if we do not use DNN but rather assume a spe cific functional form (e.g., a linear model) for β(Wi) or f(µi,τt) in the estimation, the estimated distribution of βis can be largely biased.

We first test what happens if we assume that β(·) is a linear function (see the Figure 5(a), top row).11

When the true β(Wi) is a nonlinear function of Wi, the

Surpris ingly, even when the true β(Wi) is a linear function of Wi (but includes only some elements of Wi in the function), the linear model estimation performs poorly (Figure 5(a), top left). We find that only when the true β(Wi) is linear and includes all elements of Wi (called the “linear-all” case) does the linear model accurately capture the true value of βis (Figure 5(a), top middle). The contrast between the linear and linear-all cases indi cates that linear models are poor at variable selection; that is, they cannot accurately identify which pretreat ment features’ variations contribute to the variations in βis. This explains why linear models may yield inaccu rate estimates even when the true functional form is lin ear. In contrast, when we use DNNs to estimate β(·) (in Figure 5(a), bottom row), the estimated values of βis closely approximate the true values, no matter whether the true functional relationship is linear (bottom left), linear-all (bottom middle), or nonlinear (bottom right).

In Figure 5(b), we test what happens if we assume that f(·,·) is a linear function in estimation. When the true f(·,·) is linear, which means that the true individual fixed effects and time fixed effects are just additive, the

linear model works and performs as well as using DNN to estimate the nuisance function (Figure 5(b), left column). When the true f(·,·) is nonlinear—specifically multiplicative—the linear model yields biased estimates of βi’s (Figure 5(b), top right), whereas our DNN approach still uncovers the true βi’s effectively (Figure 5(b), bottom right). To summarize, our Deep-DiD method exhibits remarkable adaptability, successfully capturing both linear and nonlinear relationships without requiring a prior specification of the functional form.

Furthermore, we compare DNN to random forests. Note that combining random forests with a DiD model with fixed effects is challenging and has not been solved as far as we know, and it is beyond the scope of this paper to address this issue.12 Thus, we set aside the DiD setting for now and focus solely on functional approximation. The comparison between the estimated and true values of βis is displayed in Figure 6, with the implementation details provided in the figure note. This figure shows that DNN outperforms random forests in uncovering true βis, demonstrating DNN’s superior performance in functional approximation compared with random forests.

theoretical expectations are closely met. Real-world scenarios often introduce more complexities and nuan ces, which may require adjustments of the architecture and hyperparameters of DNNs, including those that showed less sensitivity in our simulations.

One may wonder, in a real-world application (rather than a simulation task) where the true treat ment effects are unobservable, how we can assess the model’s performance and, furthermore, how to select the architecture and hyperparameters for the DNNs in the model. It is important to note that we are not training the model using observed treatment effects but rather using observed Yi’s. Essentially, our method estimates the individual-level treatment effect βi as a function of individual pretreatment features Wi based on the equation βi  E[Y(1)|Wi] E[Y(0)|Wi], where Y(d) ≡Y(Di  d),d  0,1. For each individual i, only one of the {Y(1),Y(0)} is observed because he or she was either treated or untreated, and the other’s expected value (as a function of Wi) is predicted by the model. More specifically, we learn the relationship between Y(d) and Wi based on the individuals whose Y(d) are observable and then predict E[Y(d)|Wi] for individuals whose Y(d) are unobservable (d  0,1). Therefore, although the final output is an estimated causal effect, our method fundamentally remains a prediction task. As with other prediction problems, performance can be evaluated using measures such as MSE, which quantify the discrepancy between predicted

ˆYis and actual Yis observed. The way of choosing the DNN architecture and hyperparameters is similar to other prediction tasks. Existing literature offers practical guidelines for these choices (see, e.g. Bengio 2012, Goodfellow et al. 2016, and Aggarwal 2018). Architec ture selection typically starts from matching the archi tecture to the data modality: Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs) for tabular data, Convolutional Neural Net works (CNNs) for images, or Recurrent Neural

Networks (RNNs) for sequential data. The selection of network depth, width, activation functions, and train ing configurations such as the optimizer (e.g., Adam, SGD) and learning rate usually requires systematic experimentation. In this process, the training and vali dation losses are closely monitored to diagnose issues like overfitting or underfitting. A simple baseline often serves as a good starting point. In the context of this paper, a baseline MLP with two to three hidden layers has proven very effective, as shown in our simulations and empirical application (Section 4).

3. Empirical Background We apply our Deep-DiD method to a real-world empirical setting to estimate the HTEs of a specific treatment. We collaborate with a large short-video sharing platform that was expanding their global user base. As part of its global growth strategy, the plat form launched a “Creator Signing Program” in three countries located in South America, Africa, and Europe. The program aimed to incentivize content creators to upload more high-quality original content to the plat form. Selected creators were able to sign a contract with the platform to join the program.13 After joining the program, they received monthly payments by the plat form based on their performance during the month. We apply our approach to estimate the HTEs of this signing program and show how our estimation results can help the platform optimize its creator selection.

We focus on creators from the three countries who were signed from May 1, 2022, to June 30, 2022.14

Because there is a very large number of unsigned creators—far too many to include all in our analyses— we construct a control group from the pool of unsigned creators (as of data collection) by matching them with signed creators. Our matching procedure is unconventional in the sense that we match on crea tors’ trends of outcome measures rather than their

mean levels. A conventional matching procedure selects untreated individuals who are similar to treated indivi duals based on observable characteristics, aiming to construct a comparable control group such that the treatment assignment is as good as random. After a conventional matching procedure, treatment effects can be estimated by directly comparing posttreatment means between treated and control groups. In our set ting, however, signed creators are systematically differ ent from unsigned creators; they generally demonstrate higher performance measures even before the treat ment. Thus, constructing a control group that is sta tistically indifferent from the treated group through conventional matching is challenging.15 Nevertheless, DiD requires only that the treated and control groups exhibit parallel trends in outcome measures before treatment, not that they be statistically indifferent before treatment.16 Therefore, we match on the trends of out come measures, aiming to construct a control group that exhibits parallel pretreatment trends with the trea ted group. In particular, for each creator who uploaded at least five videos17 from February 1 to April 30, 2022, we estimate the trend of each performance measure using a linear regression. Because signed creators have different signing dates (after May 1) and unsigned crea tors do not have signing dates, we use data in the com mon period, February 1 to April 30, to estimate the trends. Then, we conduct propensity score matching (PSM), with the estimated trends as matching variables. More details of the matching procedure are available in Online Appendix A.1.18

The matched data set comprises 2,343 creators in the signed group and 2,343 creators in the control group. In Online Appendix Table A.2, we test that the signed group and the control group have parallel pre treatment trends for all outcome measures. In particu lar, we regress the creator-day level outcome measures on Treated × # Days to Signing Date, with creator fixed effects and day fixed effects controlled for. Part A of the table uses observations from May 1, 2022, to each crea tor’s signing date. Because the matching procedure uses the data of February 1–April 30, 2022, using the data from May 1 to the signing date to test the parallel trend is an “extrapolation” test,” which can be considered as a test of the assumption that the treatment and control groups would have followed the parallel trajectories over time in the absence of treatment. Part B of the table uses an extended period from February 1, 2022, to each creator’s signing date. Both Part A and Part B show sta tistically insignificant coefficients for the interaction term Treated × # Days to Signing Date across all outcome measures, supporting the parallel-trend assumption.

For each creator, we designated their signing date as Day 0 and collected data of the 89 days before19

and 90 days after the signing date (including the sign ing date). For control group creators, we defined their

Day 0 as the signing date of their matched treated cre ator. The data we obtained included (1) creator fea tures, like the number of followers a creator has and how many users a creator is following, the creator’s gender, country, etc.; (2) creators’ production, like the number of videos a creator uploads on a day; (3) video viewing, that is, the number of views, the number of completed views, and the total play duration each video has; (4) users’ interactions (engagement beha viors), that is, the number of likes, comments, shares, and follows20 each video has, and (5) visual and audio features of each video. We will elaborate more on these variables in Sections 3.1 and 4.1, when we define and construct the outcome variables and input variables.

3.1. Outcome Variable: Measurement of Creator Performance To study the effect of the signing program on creators’ performance and how the platform should select crea tors to sign, we first need to determine how to mea sure a creator’s performance.21 The goal of the signing program is to incentivize creators to contribute more videos with original content and higher quality, and these videos in turn can attract users to spend more time and have more interactions on the platform. These make the platform a prosperous content plat form and attract more users in the long run. There fore, when choosing the key performance measures, we focus on how to measure a creator’s contribution to the platform in these aspects. Based on this princi ple and communication with managers in the com pany, we choose two key performance measures, as illustrated below.

The first performance measure is User Time Contrib uted, meaning the cumulative time length that the creator’s videos have been watched by all viewers. This measure is important to the platform because it captures how much user screen time the video contri butes to the platform, which is directly related to the platform’s profitability. The platform cares not only about how much time users spend on the platform but also about whether users get engaged and interact on the platform, which can be measured by how many likes, comments, shares, and follows a video gets. These responses reflect different degrees of user engagement (Brodie et al. 2011, Oestreicher-Singer and Zalmanson 2013, Yang et al. 2019). To offer a holistic measure of engagement, we integrate these four engagement measures by performing Principal Component Analysis (PCA) and take the first compo nent as the User Engagement measure. Therefore, we determine two key performance measures of creators, User Time Contributed and User Engagement, both of which are defined at the creator-day level.22 Table 3 presents the summary statistics of the two perfor mance measures.

Note that our approach does not hinge upon our choice of performance measures, and it can be applied easily when other measures are chosen as the outcome variable. For example, a platform may define a weighted sum of these two performance measures as the single key performance measure. Then they can easily calculate that measure and use it as the outcome variable when applying our method.

3.2. Impact of the Signing Program on Creator Performance We first graphically show the effect of the signing pro gram on creator performance. For each performance measure, Figure 7 shows its daily average value of creators in the signed group versus in the control group in the 89 days before and 90 days after Day 0.

We can see that the signed group has a significant jump in both performance measures after Day 0, and both performance measures are relatively stable in the 90 days after Day 0, implying that the positive impacts on User Time Contributed and User Engagement of signed creators tend to be long-lasting.

To quantify the impact of the signing program on creator performance, we conduct DiD analyses as sug gested by model (1), as shown in Table 4. Columns (1) and (3) report the results when the Treated dummy (Di) and After dummy (At) are included in the regres sion, and Columns (2) and (4) show the results when creator and day fixed effects are controlled for. For both performance measures, the coefficients of the

interaction term are positive and statistically signifi cant, and their magnitudes are relatively stable after we control for fixed effects.23 The relative effect size of the treatment is larger than 100% for both perfor mance measures. To summarize, the DiD regression results show that the signing program has a signifi cant and substantial positive impact on signed crea tors’ performance, which is measured by the amount of user watching time and engagement contributed by the videos.

4. Using Deep-DiD to Estimate the Heterogeneous Treatment Effects of the Signing Program Now we apply the Deep-DiD method to the empirical setting to estimate the heterogeneous treatment effects of the signing program.

In Section 4.1, we describe how we construct crea tors’ pretreatment characteristics Wi. In Section 4.2, we provide the details of the model estimation techni ques and estimation results.

4.1. Creators’ Pretreatment Features We construct the pretreatment features of creators Wi, utilizing the rich data we have as much as possible. We not only make use of the structured data describ ing creators’ production behaviors and viewers’ responses but also utilize the video and audio features, which are derived from unstructured video data using

deep-learning-based methods. We encountered some data loss in this process because some videos had been deleted by creators and become unavailable for downloading. We remove the creators who have more than 10% of videos missing. After this step, we are left with 2,204 creators, among which 1,126 are from the treated group and 1,078 are from the control group. The results of conventional DiD analyses based on this reduced data set (see Online Appendix A.3) are very close to the full sample results as shown in Figure 7 and Table 4.

In the following, we describe how we construct variables in Wi. We classify the creator features into three categories: (1) creators’ production behavior and viewers’ responses, (2) visual features, and (3) audio features.

For the first category, creators’ production behavior and viewers’ responses, we include variables that describe a creator’s production quantity (Production, meaning the number of videos uploaded on the day), viewers’ viewing behavior (Num of Plays, meaning how many times the creator’s videos were played by viewers on the day; Num of Complete Plays, meaning how many times the creator’s videos were watched by viewers from the beginning to the end on the day; and Play Duration, meaning the total time length that the creator’s videos were watched by viewers on the day), and viewers’ interactions with the creator (Num of

Likes, Num of Comments, Num of Shares, Num of Follows, meaning the total number of likes, comments, shares, and follows the creator’s videos get on the day). We also include variables that describe the creator’s account status on the platform: how many followers the creator has on the day (Num of Followers) and how many users the creator is following on the day (Num of Following Users). To reduce the dimension of Wi, we aggregate these variables from the creator-day level to the creator level by taking the mean, median, mini mum (min), maximum (max), and standard deviation (SD) of each variable for each creator, using observa tions in the 89 days before the signing date. Further more, to capture the trend of changes, we also calculate the slope of each variable for each creator to include in Wi. The slope of a variable captures whether and by how much this variable is increasing, decreasing, or remaining relatively steady for a creator.

A video can be considered as a combination of a large number of consecutive images plus audio. The manner in which the content is visually and aurally presented to the audience can directly impact users’ watching experience and thus can influence their will ingness to continue watching and get engaged (see, e.g., Li et al. 2019, Hwang et al. 2021, Wang et al. 2021, Zhou et al. 2021, Cheng and Zhang 2024, and Yang et al. 2025). Having access to the videos uploaded by creators, we are able to extract visual and audio fea tures from them to be included in Wi. For visual fea tures, we use eight visual quality measures, including Blur Probability, Blocky Probability, Dirty Lens Probabil ity, Noise Probability, Colorfulness, Defocus Probability, Aesthetic Score, and Quality Score, as well as one simi larity measure for each video. For audio features, we include five measures, which are Audio Quality, Stereo phonic Richness, Background Noise Probability, Dialog Probability, and Music probability. For each visual fea ture and audio feature, we aggregate these video level measures to the creator level as the model input; for each creator and each measure, we take the mean, median, min, max, and SD of the measure on all the videos uploaded by the creator in the 89 days before the signing date and include these five summary sta tistics in Wi.

In Online Appendix A.4, we provide more detailed explanations of the variables mentioned above, why we choose them, and how we calculate them as well as their summary statistics.

Because many of the variables in pretreatment fea tures Wi can be largely skewed or have outliers, feed ing them to the input layer of the DNN may result in gradient explosion. Therefore, before feeding Wi into the model, we preprocess the data using winsoriza tion,24 log-transformation, and min-max normalization methods. These preprocessing steps are commonly used in deep learning, and they help to avoid gradient explosion and ensure a smooth convergence. More details of the data-preprocessing procedures are avail able in Online Appendix A.5.

We randomly split our data into two parts, 60% (1,322 creators) for model training and validation and 40% (882 creators) for out-of-sample testing. Within the first part, 80% of the observations are for model training, and 20% are for validation.25 The loss func tion we use is the mean squared error (MSE). In the training process, we monitor the reported loss on the validation set to prevent overfitting. We use the Adam optimizer and adopt a learning rate of 0.001. We choose the batch size as 512 and the number of

epochs as 20. We design three fully connected hidden layers of (128, 64, 32) neurons activated by the ReLU function. Note that in the model training process, the number of individuals N  1,322, the number of pre treatment features J  130, and the total time periods T  179. According to our simulation results shown in Section 2.1.2, with this size of data, the Deep-DiD model is able to uncover the true distribution of βis with fairly high accuracy under proper implementa tion choices.

As illustrated in Section 2.1.1, the trained model provides us with an estimated function ˆβ(·). We can apply it to calculate ˆβi  ˆβ(Wi) for each i in the training-validation set and the test set. To mitigate the randomness in the model training process, we per form the model training 10 times, each time initialized with a different random seed. For each i, we take the average value of ˆβi across these 10 rounds as the final estimated value of ˆβi.26 The convergence plot in one of the 10 rounds is presented in Online Appendix A.5. 5. Creator Selection Now we show how our method can help the platform identify the right creators to sign and whether it out performs platform selection. The idea is straightfor ward. The goal of signing a creator is to incentivize the creator to improve his or her performance. Our model estimation gives ˆβ(Wi), that is, the estimated treatment effect of the signing program on each indi vidual creator’s performance as a function of his or her pretreatment features Wi. Given a new set of crea tors, the platform can calculate their estimated treat ment effects ˆβis based on our estimated function ˆβ(·) and their pretreatment features Wis. Suppose the plat form plans to select K creators out of this set of crea tors; it would then simply select the top K creators with the highest ˆβis.

5.1. Creator Selection by Deep-DiD Model vs. Platform Selection We test the performance of our estimated model on creator selection using the test set (i.e., out-of-sample). Among the 882 creators in the test set, 441 of them are from the signed group. We label them as Platform Selected. To compare the performance of our method to that of platform selection, we identify the same number (441) of creators with the highest βis from the 882 creators in the test sample and label them as Model Selected. Here, we set the number of Model Selected creators the same as that of the Platform Selected ones so that the comparison between the two groups is fair. The fewer creators we select, the higher the selection bar (in terms of the estimated treatment effects) can be. Because we have no access to information regard ing the exact cost and monetary benefit of signing a creator, we cannot determine the optimal number of creators to sign.

Among the 441 Model Selected creators based on ˆβis when the performance measure is User Time Contrib uted, 248 are from the signed group. When the perfor mance measure is User Engagement, among the Model Selected creators, 225 are from the signed group. For both performance measures, nearly 50% of the Model Selected creators were not selected by the platform.

As a first evaluation, we compare the average esti mated treatment effects (the mean of ˆβis) of Model Selected versus Platform Selected creators. As shown in Figure 9(a), for both performance measures, the Model Selected creators have substantially higher average estimated treatment effects than the Platform Selected creators.

One may argue that the comparison above is not a fair comparison because Model Selected creators are selected based on ˆβis, and thus, it is not surprising that they have higher average ˆβis than Platform Selected creators, although the magnitude of the dif ference cannot be predicted ex ante. To resolve this concern, we come up with a second way to evaluate the performance of our method. For each creator who was actually signed, we can observe how much his or her performance changed after he or she got signed. We define the creator’s average daily performance after the signing date minus that before the signing date as the creator’s Performance Jump, which can be considered as the empirically observed “treatment effect” of the creator. The Performance Jump can also be negative if the creator’s average daily performance decreased. We divide the 441 signed creators in the test set into two groups:27 those who are also selected by the model and those who are not selected by the model. We calculate the average performance jump (APJ) for each of these two groups as well as for all 441 signed creators (see Table 5, Part A). We calculate the percentage difference between the APJ of creators selected by the model versus that of all signed crea tors. For both performance measures, the APJs of those selected by the model are substantially larger than those not selected by the model. The percentage difference in APJ between creators selected by the model and all signed creators is above 70% for both performance measures. This evaluation provides fur ther empirical evidence for the superior performance of our method compared with platform selection. That is, the Model Selected creators not only have higher estimated treatment effects of the signing pro gram, their actual increase in performance after being signed is also significantly larger than the platform selected ones.

In Online Appendix A.6, we conduct in-sample tests showing that among the 1,322 creators in the training-validation set, Model Selected creators also outperform Platform Selected creators.

We also calculate the APJ for creators selected by the linear model among all signed creators in the test set and compare it to those not selected by the model as well as all signed creators. Results are provided in Table 5, part B. Comparing the percentage differences listed in part B with those in part A, we find that for both performance measures, our Deep-DiD model leads to a larger improvement in APJ than the linear model. When the outcome measure is User Time Con tributed, the linear model even leads to lower APJ compared with all signed creators.

The comparisons above demonstrate the superiority of our Deep-DiD model versus the linear model. We can see that the Deep-DiD model performs consis tently better than the linear model and demonstrates more robust performances across different outcome measures.

Note that the linear model here is estimated in a more modern way than the traditional ordinary least squares (OLS) method; we employ our Deep-DiD model framework but assume both the HTE estima tion network and the fixed-effect network as single- layer (i.e., the input layer connects directly to the output layer without hidden layers). This is equiva lent to assuming that β(·) is linear and the fixed effects are additive. It is mathematically equivalent to OLS because both methods minimize mean squared errors. However, compared with traditional OLS, estimating the linear model by training one-layer neural net works is much more computationally and memory efficient because the data are processed batch by batch and the model’s weights are updated iteratively. This avoids the need to load the entire data set into mem ory and perform a single, massive matrix inversion, as what traditional OLS does. Therefore, our model framework can incorporate the linear model as a spe cial case, and the estimation algorithm makes it

possible to deal with large-scale, high-dimensional data. If estimating the linear model using traditional OLS, we are likely to encounter dimensional explosion because the model contains 130 three-way interaction terms Wij ∗Di ∗At (j  1,:::,J, where J  130) as well as high-dimensional individual (N1,322) and time (T  179) fixed effects. We may have to reduce the number of pretreatment features included in the model, which may further lower the performance of the linear model.

5.3. Visualization of Model Selected vs. Platform Selected Creators Next we try to visualize how Model Selected creators may differ from those Platform Selected creators. As shown in Figure 10, we choose two representative dimensions in each feature category and visualize the two groups of creators on a two-dimensional plane. We use red dots to represent Model Selected creators, blue dots to represent Platform Selected creators, and gray dots to represent the overlapping creators (i.e., selected both by the model and by the platform). Here, we show only the comparison when the model selection is based on User Time Contributed as the out come variable. An interesting observation from Figure 10(a) is that human selection tends to select creators with a larger number of followers, whereas the model tends to select creators with a lower number of followers. However, in Figure 10, (b) and (c), we find it hard to observe a pattern in terms of whether Model Selected creators tend to be higher or lower in a certain feature. This highlights the advantages and importance of the DNN approach. The fact that it is hard to separate Model Selected creators and Platform Selected creators with a line on a two-dimensional plane implies that

6. Concluding Remarks In this paper, we propose a Deep-DiD model that incorporates two DNN structures in a DiD framework to estimate HTEs. We conduct a series of simulations showing that our approach can uncover the true values of HTEs with high accuracy. Furthermore, we apply our method to an empirical setting to estimate the HTEs of a “Creator Signing Program” launched by a large video-sharing platform and use the esti mated HTEs to optimize creator selection for the plat form. We show that compared with creators selected by the platform, creators selected by our model have not only higher estimated treatment effects but also higher actual performance jumps after being signed. Creator selection based on the Deep-DiD model also demonstrates consistently better performance than that based on linear models.

To the best of our knowledge, our paper represents the first implementation of the DNN-based heteroge neity architecture proposed by Farrell et al. (2020) in a real empirical context. We innovatively integrate two DNN structures with the DiD framework, setting up a dual-network architecture to allow for flexible non parametric relationships between the HTEs and pre treatment features, as well as possible interactions between fixed effects. We demonstrate the perfor mance of this method through simulations.

Through the empirical application, we demonstrate the significant potential for managerial applications of our approach. Platforms or influencer agency compa nies can initiate a pilot signing program and utilize data from this program in conjunction with our Deep- DiD model to estimate the expected treatment effect of the signing program on individual creators’ perfor mance as a function of their pretreatment features. Then, they can automate the process of creator selec tion by targeting those with the highest estimated treatment effects.

The application of our method extends beyond this context. Our method can be easily tailored to other empirical settings, especially those with a rich data set, to estimate the HTEs of a certain treatment. Researchers can flexibly define the pretreatment fea tures and the outcome variable. We have demonstrated that our method can uncover the true distribution of HTEs with high accuracy under various settings, and

the estimated HTEs can help optimize the selection of individuals to be treated in the future.

A limitation of our method is that we cannot provide standard errors for the estimated treatment effects. It is still unknown whether the estimated individual-level heterogeneity has traditional consistency and asymp totic statistical properties (Farrell et al. 2020). Our focus is not on the statistical significance of treatment effects but on how they vary with individuals’ pretreatment features, which enables targeting or selection based on pretreatment features, such as the creator selection application demonstrated in this paper or customer tar geting for profit-maximizing (see, e.g., Simester et al. 2020 and Hitsch et al. 2024). Statistical inference is pos sible for functions of the estimated individual-level heterogeneity under certain conditions (Chernozhukov et al. 2018, Farrell et al. 2020), and thus, it is possible to derive standard errors for profits of targeting policies (Zhang 2024). This can be a future research direction.

Second, our large sample sizes lead to consistent statistical significance, even for negligible differences. This is a well-known “large n problem” in hypothesis testing. Thus, we focus on the KS statistic and JS diver gence as more informative measures of distributional differences rather than conducting hypothesis tests.

16 Note that the conventional DiD model can address both timeinvariant (e.g., inherent abilities, family background) and time- variant unobservable confounders (e.g., platform popularity, economic shifts, policy changes). Time-varying confounders affecting all units equally or randomly are differenced out in the first-stage differenc ing (over time) in DiD. Time-invariant gaps between treatment and control groups are differenced out in the second-stage differencing (across units). We have also verified that our Deep-DiD model can address these two types of confounders through simulations, as shown in Figure 4. Time-varying confounders specific to the treated group posttreatment (e.g., positive feedback loop) cannot be differ enced out but are of interest to the platform and researchers as part of the overall treatment effect.

17 This threshold is necessary because trends are poorly defined for creators with too few videos in the pretreatment period. Although five videos are not ideal, setting a higher threshold would severely limit our sample size.

18 Our matching procedure shares a similar spirit with the synthetic DiD method proposed by Arkhangelsky et al. (2021). Both methods aim to construct a control group with a parallel pretreatment trend relative to the treated group based on the idea that DiD requires parallel trends rather than statistical indifference in pretreatment outcomes. We choose not to use the synthetic DiD method for matching because its computationally intensive weighting and reg ularization parameters would have overcomplicated the implemen tation of our Deep-DiD method. Note that this matching procedure is not central to our Deep-DiD method; its sole purpose is to con struct a control group from a very large pool of untreated units. In future applications, if the data set already has treated and control groups satisfying the parallel-trend condition, then our Deep-DiD method can be applied directly. If matching is needed, what match ing method and matching variables to use depends on the specific empirical context.

19 We have access to data from February 1, 2022, onward. For crea tors signed on May 1, 2022, we have 89 days of pre-signing data (February 1 to April 30).

20 The number of “follows” a video gets means how many users decide to follow the creator after watching the video.

21 We do not know what measures the platform uses to evaluate the impact of this signing program, nor do we have access to the exact formula the platform uses to calculate each creator’s payment. Thus, we do not have a well-defined set of performance measures at hand and need to define the key performance measures by our selves based on our understanding of the primary goals of the platform.

22 For User Time Contributed, we first calculate it for each video by aggregating the total watch time a video gets in the first 20 days fol lowing the video’s release, because based on historical data, usually a video gets most exposures in the first 20 days after release. Then, we aggregate it to the creator-day level by summing up the values of videos created by the creator on that day. The main reason for this handling is that the outcome variables are to capture the contri bution a creator made to the platform on a day by uploading videos. If a creator has no videos uploaded on a day, then the vari able value is 0 for this creator on that day. For User Engagement, we first follow the same procedure to aggregate each of the four inter action metrics (likes, comments, shares, and follows) from video- level to creator-day level and then conduct PCA. Factor loadings of the four components are reported in Online Appendix A.2.
